title: Database Access Concepts
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of database access concepts in a C#/.NET program.
Predict the result of the included C# example and verify the documented output.
Apply database access concepts to a small task and identify one relevant boundary, limitation, or version requirement.

content.intro: Database Access Concepts is lesson 153 in APIs, Networking, and Database Integration. Integration code should isolate network or database calls, use parameters instead of string-built commands, validate external data, and define transaction boundaries.
content.why_it_matters: External systems fail and return untrusted data, so integration code needs timeouts, validation, and clear data boundaries. This lesson focuses on database access concepts and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Integration code should isolate network or database calls, use parameters instead of string-built commands, validate external data, and define transaction boundaries.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for database access concepts. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

items.title: Relational databases and tables
items.text: Use explicit timeouts, parameterized database commands, small service boundaries, and validation for external results.

items.title: Database connections

items.title: Queries and parameters
items.text: Pick a parameter-passing form that communicates ownership and intent; avoid ref/out when a returned value is clearer.

items.title: Reading query results
items.text: Break the query into readable stages and verify the source, predicate, projection, ordering, and materialization point.

items.title: Connection management
items.text: For connection management, define the expected behavior, inspect how it relates to database access concepts, and verify a representative case plus one boundary or failure case.

items.title: Transactions and consistency
items.text: Treat HTTP and database responses as untrusted boundaries. Set timeouts, check status codes, parameterize SQL, validate deserialized results, and make transaction scope and disposal explicit.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates database access concepts. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates database access concepts rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for database access concepts before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
